title: String Length, charAt, and indexOf
description: Use String methods to inspect individual characters and find the position of substrings. Practice length(), charAt(int index), indexOf(String str), and lastIndexOf(String str).
hints: length() returns an int — the total number of chars including spaces and punctuation.
charAt(index) is zero-based; charAt(0) returns 'H' for "Hello".
indexOf returns -1 when the substring is not found — useful for existence checks.

solution.explanation: length() counts all characters, including spaces, commas, and punctuation — 'Hello, Java World!' has 18. charAt(7) returns 'J' because indexing starts at 0: H(0) e(1) l(2) l(3) o(4) ,(5) (6) J(7). indexOf('o') scans left-to-right and stops at the first match (index 4 in 'Hello'). lastIndexOf('o') scans right-to-left, finding 'o' in 'World' at 13. indexOf returns -1 for any substring not present — this is the standard sentinel value Java uses for 'not found'.

methodSignatures.description: Returns the number of characters in the string.
Returns the char at the given zero-based index; throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException if out of range.
Returns the index of the first occurrence of str, or -1 if not found.
Returns the index of the last occurrence of str, or -1 if not found.

title: substring, contains, startsWith, endsWith
description: Extract portions of strings with substring() and check membership/position with contains(), startsWith(), and endsWith().
hints: substring(start, end) extracts characters from start (inclusive) to end (exclusive).
substring(start) extracts from start to the end of the string.
Combine indexOf() with substring() to locate and extract dynamic portions.

solution.explanation: substring(0, schemeEnd) extracts characters at indices 0 through schemeEnd-1. Because indexOf("://") returns 5 for 'https', substring(0,5) gives 'https'. contains(), startsWith(), and endsWith() all return booleans and are convenience wrappers — internally they use indexOf or char comparison. To find the path we skip past '://' (3 chars) so we don't accidentally match the slashes in the scheme, then look for the next '/' which starts the path. substring(pathStart) with one argument goes to the end of the string.

methodSignatures.description: Returns a new string from beginIndex to end.
Returns a new string from beginIndex (inclusive) to endIndex (exclusive).
Returns true if the string contains the given sequence.
Returns true if the string begins with the given prefix.
Returns true if the string ends with the given suffix.

title: isEmpty vs isBlank (Java 11)
description: Understand the distinction between isEmpty() and isBlank(), and how they handle whitespace-only strings.
hints: isEmpty() returns true only when length() == 0.
isBlank() (Java 11+) returns true when the string is empty OR contains only whitespace characters.
isBlank() uses Character.isWhitespace() which covers tabs, newlines, and Unicode spaces.

solution.explanation: isEmpty() is a simple length check: only the zero-length string returns true. isBlank() was introduced in Java 11 to fill a common need: detecting 'effectively empty' strings that contain only whitespace. A string of spaces or tabs is not empty (length > 0) but is blank (no visible content). isBlank() is equivalent to strip().isEmpty() — strip() uses Unicode-aware whitespace rules, unlike trim() which only strips ASCII control chars <= '\u0020'. Always prefer isBlank() over isEmpty() when validating user input.

methodSignatures.description: Returns true if and only if length() == 0.
Java 11+. Returns true if the string is empty or contains only whitespace (Unicode-aware).

title: Case Conversion: toUpperCase and toLowerCase
description: Convert string casing using toUpperCase() and toLowerCase(), including locale-sensitive variants.
hints: toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() without arguments use the default JVM locale — safe for most English text.
For code identifiers or protocol strings, always pass Locale.ROOT to avoid locale-specific surprises.
To capitalise a single character: Character.toUpperCase(char c).

solution.explanation: toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() produce new String objects; Strings in Java are immutable so no modification happens in place. The locale issue with Turkish 'I' is a real production bug: Turkish locale maps uppercase 'I' -> 'İ' (with dot) and 'i' -> 'İ', while lowercase 'I' -> 'ı' (no dot). Code that compares HTTP header names or XML tags using the default locale on a Turkish server will silently break. Always use Locale.ROOT for programmatic strings. Only use the default locale when displaying text to the user.

methodSignatures.description: Converts all characters to uppercase using the default locale.
Converts all characters to uppercase using the specified locale.
Converts all characters to lowercase using the specified locale.

title: trim() vs strip() — Whitespace Removal
description: Understand the difference between legacy trim() and Java 11's strip() / stripLeading() / stripTrailing() for removing whitespace.
hints: trim() treats any character with code point <= '\u0020' (space) as whitespace.
strip() uses Character.isWhitespace() which handles Unicode whitespace (\u00A0, \u2009, etc.).
stripLeading() and stripTrailing() are Java 11+ and allow asymmetric stripping.

solution.explanation: trim() was written in Java 1.0 before Unicode was well understood. It removes everything with a code point <= 32 (the ASCII space). Non-breaking space (\u00A0 = 160) is above that threshold, so trim() leaves it in place. strip() (Java 11) delegates to Character.isWhitespace() which correctly identifies all Unicode whitespace categories. For new code, always prefer strip(). stripLeading() and stripTrailing() are useful when you only want to normalise one side — for example, parsing indented config file lines where leading indentation is significant but a trailing newline is not.

methodSignatures.description: Removes leading and trailing characters with code point <= '\u0020'.
Java 11+. Removes leading and trailing Unicode whitespace.
Java 11+. Removes leading Unicode whitespace only.
Java 11+. Removes trailing Unicode whitespace only.

title: replace, replaceAll, replaceFirst
description: Replace substrings using literal replacement (replace) and regex-based replacement (replaceAll, replaceFirst).
hints: replace(CharSequence, CharSequence) does plain literal replacement, no regex.
replaceAll(String regex, String replacement) and replaceFirst() interpret the first argument as a regex.
In a regex passed to replaceAll, backslashes must be double-escaped: \\d means the regex \d (digit).

solution.explanation: replace(CharSequence old, CharSequence new) treats both arguments as literal strings — no regex magic. This is safer when your replacement text might contain regex metacharacters like '$' or '\'. replaceAll() compiles its first argument as a regex each call; for hot loops consider pre-compiling with Pattern.compile(). The regex \\d+ in a Java string literal becomes \d+ at runtime, matching one or more digits. ,+ matches one or more consecutive commas, so replaceAll(",+", ",") collapses runs of commas.

methodSignatures.description: Replaces all literal occurrences of target with replacement.
Replaces every substring matching the regex with replacement.
Replaces the first substring matching the regex with replacement.

title: split() with regex and limit
description: Split strings using regex delimiters and control the number of parts with the limit parameter.
hints: split() with no limit removes trailing empty strings; split(regex, -1) keeps them.
A limit of n means at most n parts; the last part contains the remainder (unsplit).
To split on a literal dot, escape it: split("\\.") — a bare '.' matches any char.

solution.explanation: split() discards trailing empty tokens by default (limit=0). Passing -1 preserves them — important when parsing fixed-format CSV where trailing fields matter. A positive limit n caps the result at n parts; the last element holds the rest of the string unsplit. The dot pitfall is a very common bug: '.' is a regex wildcard matching any character, so "192.168.1.1".split(".") produces an empty array because every position matches. You must escape it as "\\.". Similarly, '|', '*', '+', '?' and other metacharacters need escaping when you mean them literally — or use Pattern.quote(str) to auto-escape.

methodSignatures.description: Splits around matches of regex; trailing empty strings are discarded.
Splits with at most limit parts; negative limit keeps trailing empty strings.

title: String.join() and String.format() / formatted()
description: Join collections of strings with a delimiter using String.join(), and format strings using String.format() and the Java 15 instance method formatted().
hints: String.join(delimiter, elements...) is a static method — it never produces a leading or trailing delimiter.
String.format() uses printf-style specifiers: %s (string), %d (int), %f (float), %n (newline).
%-15s means left-align in a 15-char field; %.2f means 2 decimal places; %06d means pad to 6 with zeros.

solution.explanation: String.join() is much cleaner than a StringBuilder loop with manual delimiter tracking. It handles empty arrays gracefully (returns "") and never adds a spurious leading or trailing delimiter. String.format() is equivalent to sprintf in C — the format string is compiled each call. The format specifiers: %-15s is left-aligned ('-') string in a 15-wide field; %.2f rounds and formats a float/double to 2 decimal places; %06d pads an integer to 6 characters with zeros. The Java 15 formatted() method does exactly the same as String.format(pattern, args) but reads more naturally as it's called on the format string itself — useful in fluent chains.

methodSignatures.description: Joins elements with delimiter between each pair.

methodSignatures.method: String String.join(CharSequence delimiter, Iterable<? extends CharSequence> elements)
methodSignatures.description: Joins an Iterable of strings with delimiter.
Returns a formatted string using printf-style specifiers.
Java 15+. Instance method equivalent to String.format(this, args).

title: StringBuilder: append, insert, delete, replace
description: Build and modify strings efficiently using StringBuilder's mutable operations.
hints: insert(int offset, String str) inserts at the given offset, shifting subsequent chars right.
delete(int start, int end) removes chars from start (inclusive) to end (exclusive).
replace(int start, int end, String str) replaces the range [start,end) with str.

solution.explanation: StringBuilder is a mutable sequence of characters backed by a resizable char array. All mutating methods (append, insert, delete, replace) return 'this', so you can chain them: sb.append("a").append("b"). insert(offset, str) shifts all characters at or after offset to the right by str.length() — O(n) operation. delete(start, end) closes the gap in-place — also O(n). replace(start, end, str) removes [start, end) and inserts str at start — the replacement can be a different length, so the buffer may grow or shrink. indexOf() on StringBuilder works the same as on String.

methodSignatures.description: Appends str to the end; returns this for chaining.
Inserts str at the given position; shifts existing chars right.
Removes chars from start (inclusive) to end (exclusive).

methodSignatures.method: StringBuilder StringBuilder.replace(int start, int end, String str)
methodSignatures.description: Replaces [start, end) with str.

title: StringBuilder Performance: Why Not Use + in Loops
description: Demonstrate why string concatenation with '+' inside a loop is O(n²) and how StringBuilder reduces it to O(n). Includes reverse().
hints: String is immutable: s += x creates a brand-new String object, copying all existing chars plus x.
For n iterations, the total characters copied is 0+1+2+...+(n-1) = O(n²).
StringBuilder pre-allocates a buffer and amortises resizing, giving O(n) total time.
StringBuilder.reverse() reverses the buffer in-place — easiest way to reverse a string in Java.

solution.explanation: Every string concatenation with '+' allocates a new char[] and copies all existing characters into it. After n iterations, the string has length proportional to n, so the total copy work is 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2 — classic O(n²) behaviour. For n=100,000 this means ~5 billion character copies. StringBuilder maintains a growing internal char[] (like ArrayList). Appending a short value is amortised O(1) — the buffer doubles when full, so total resizing work is O(n). Providing an initial capacity hint (new StringBuilder(n * 4)) avoids most resizing entirely. Note: the Java compiler optimises compile-time string concatenation (like "Hello" + " World") but NOT concatenation inside loops.

methodSignatures.description: Reverses the character sequence in-place; returns this.
Creates a StringBuilder with a pre-allocated initial buffer of given capacity.
Returns the current contents as an immutable String.

title: equals() vs == and compareTo()
description: Understand why == compares references (not content) for Strings, and how equals(), equalsIgnoreCase(), and compareTo() work correctly.
hints: == on objects compares memory addresses, not content. Two 'new String()' calls always produce different objects.
String literals are interned: "hello" always returns the same pooled object, so == may accidentally return true.
compareTo() returns 0 (equal), negative (this < other), or positive (this > other).
Never use == to compare String content — always use equals().

solution.explanation: Java strings are objects. == tests whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory. String literals are stored in the JVM string pool and interned, so c == d is true because both literals point to the same pooled 'hello'. But new String("hello") explicitly bypasses the pool and creates a fresh heap object, so a == b is false even though the content is identical. This is why ALWAYS using equals() for string comparison is critical — pool internment is an implementation detail you should never rely on. compareTo() returns a negative integer if the receiver string would sort before the argument, zero if equal, and a positive integer if it would sort after. Arrays.sort uses this contract internally.

methodSignatures.description: Returns true if other is a String with the same characters.
Case-insensitive equality check.
Lexicographic comparison; returns <0, 0, or >0.
Case-insensitive lexicographic comparison.

title: String.intern() and the String Pool
description: Understand how intern() moves a heap string into the pool to enable reference equality, and when this matters for memory and performance.
hints: intern() looks up the string in the pool; if found, returns the pooled reference; if not, adds it and returns it.
After interning, two strings with equal content will be the same reference (==).
Use intern() sparingly — it keeps strings in the pool (PermGen/Metaspace) until the JVM exits.

solution.explanation: The JVM maintains a string pool (part of Metaspace since Java 8). All string literals are automatically interned at class load time. intern() returns the canonical representation: if an equal string is already in the pool, that reference is returned; otherwise the string is added. After interning, == can safely compare string contents because all equal strings are the same object. This is useful for memory deduplication when loading large datasets with many repeated values (e.g. enum-like strings in log data). However, interned strings are GC roots and survive until the JVM exits, so over-interning unique strings wastes metaspace. Java 8 introduced String deduplication in G1GC (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication) as a lower-risk alternative.

methodSignatures.description: Returns the canonical pool representation of the string; equal strings will return the same object.

title: Pattern, Matcher: find(), group(), replaceAll()
description: Use java.util.regex.Pattern and Matcher to compile regexes once, find all matches, extract groups, and perform replacements.
hints: Pattern.compile(regex) compiles once; Matcher matcher = pattern.matcher(input) creates a stateful cursor.
matcher.find() advances and returns true on each successive match.
matcher.group(0) is the full match; matcher.group(1) is the first capturing group (...).
String.matches(regex) requires the ENTIRE string to match — it is anchored with ^ and $.

solution.explanation: Pattern.compile() parses and compiles the regex into an internal automaton — this is the expensive step. By compiling once and calling matcher() many times you avoid recompilation per call (unlike String.replaceAll() which recompiles each call). Matcher.find() advances through the input, returning true each time a match is found. group(0) returns the full match; group(n) returns the nth capturing group (parentheses in the pattern). String.matches() secretly wraps the pattern with ^ and $ so the entire input must match — it returns false if your pattern appears anywhere within a longer string. To check containment use Pattern/Matcher.find() instead. The email regex shown is simplified; RFC 5321 fully-compliant email validation is extremely complex.

Creates a Matcher that applies this pattern to input.
Advances the cursor and returns true if the next match is found.
Returns the subsequence captured by the given group in the last match.

title: Reverse a String and Check Palindrome
description: Implement string reversal and palindrome detection. A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards (e.g. 'racecar', 'A man a plan a canal Panama').
hints: StringBuilder.reverse() is the easiest reversal approach.
For simple palindrome: check if s.equals(reverse(s)).
For the sentence variant: strip non-alpha chars with replaceAll("[^a-zA-Z]", ""), lowercase, then check.

solution.explanation: The two-pointer approach avoids creating a reversed copy of the entire string — we compare the first and last characters, then move inward. If any pair doesn't match we return false immediately (short-circuit). This is O(n/2) time and O(1) extra space. The StringBuilder.reverse() approach is simpler to write and also O(n) time, but uses O(n) extra space for the reversed string. For the 'ignore non-alpha' variant, replaceAll("[^a-zA-Z]", "") strips everything that is NOT a letter (the ^ inside [...] negates the character class), then we lowercase and run the same algorithm. This correctly handles 'A man a plan a canal Panama' (removing spaces) and ignores punctuation in strings like 'Was it a car or a cat I saw?'.

methodSignatures.description: Removes or replaces substrings matching the regex.

title: Count Vowels, Word Frequency, Anagram Check, Most Frequent Character
description: Implement four common string algorithms: counting vowels, counting word occurrences, checking if two strings are anagrams, and finding the most frequent character.
hints: For vowels, use "aeiou".indexOf(ch) != -1 after converting the char to lowercase.
For word frequency, split on \\s+ and use a HashMap with getOrDefault.
For anagram check, sort both strings and compare — or use a frequency int[26] array.
For most frequent, iterate once to build a frequency map, then iterate again (or find max in one pass).

solution.explanation: countVowels: toCharArray() gives us a char[] to iterate; checking toLowerCase ensures 'A' and 'a' both count. wordFrequency: getOrDefault(key, 0) avoids a NullPointerException when the word is seen for the first time — it's the idiomatic alternative to if(!map.containsKey(key)) map.put(key, 0). LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order so the output is stable. isAnagram: The freq int[26] approach is O(n) time and O(1) space (26 fixed slots). We increment for each char in s1 and decrement for each char in s2; if any slot is non-zero the strings have different character counts. Sorting approach is O(n log n) and allocates new arrays — less optimal. mostFrequent: We use LinkedHashMap so that when two chars tie in count, Collections.max returns the first-encountered one (insertion order breaks ties). Collections.max iterates the entry set and finds the entry with the maximum value.

methodSignatures.description: Returns a new char[] containing the characters of the string.
Returns the mapped value, or defaultValue if the key is absent.
Returns the maximum element according to the comparator.

title: Regex: Email Validation and Digit Extraction Patterns
description: Build practical regex patterns for validating email addresses and extracting numeric sequences from text. Understand common character classes and quantifiers.
hints: Email: [\w._%+-]+ matches the local part; [\w.-]+ matches the domain; \.[a-zA-Z]{2,} matches the TLD.
To extract signed integers: use pattern -?\\d+ and Matcher.find() in a loop.
IPv4: each octet is (25[0-5]|2[0-4]\\d|[01]?\\d\\d?); four of them joined by escaped dots.

solution.explanation: EMAIL_PATTERN: ^ and $ anchor the match to the whole string. [\\w._%+\\-]+ matches the local part (word chars, dots, underscores, percent, plus, hyphen — all valid in local parts). @[\\w.\\-]+ matches the domain. \\.[a-zA-Z]{2,} requires a dot followed by at least 2 letters for the TLD. INT_PATTERN: -? makes the minus optional; \\d+ matches one or more digits. The pattern will match '5' in '5abc' which is fine for extraction. IPv4: The OCTET pattern uses alternation with the most specific branch first — 25[0-5] matches 250-255, 2[0-4]\\d matches 200-249, [01]?\\d{1,2} matches 0-199. If the least-specific were first, '250' might match as '2' then '50' separately. Compiling patterns as static final fields is best practice — compile once at class load time.

methodSignatures.description: Creates a Matcher to apply this pattern to the given input.
Returns true if the entire input matches the pattern.
Returns the full matched subsequence from the last find()/matches() call.
